Abstract
This work addresses in detail the anthology Mikveh Israel by Rabbi Israel Costa (Livorno 1851). The book is one of the first educational readers for Jewish children.
The anthology contains 100 untitled stories without classification into subgroups. The
work divides the book into seven content groups and each story is given a title.
The seven groups are:
A. Biographies of Jewish personalities – 11 stories
B. Exemplary figures of Jews and non-Jews – 11 stories
C. Stories designed to instill admirable virtues in children – 23 stories
D. Stories depicting the life of children in the family, in school, and in the peer
group – 17 stories
E. Stories that show that Jews throughout history have observed their religion
in the face of edicts by foreign rulers, and were willing to [die for Kiddush Hashem] endure martyrdom – 10 stories
F. Stories that show that Gentiles were not impressed by Jews who converted
or tried to assimilate, and commended Jews who preserved their Jewish or religious identity – 8 stories
G. Stories that represent the Jewish religion through its beliefs and positions, emphasize
the centrality of prayer, and address theological issues – 20 stories.
The theological issues addressed are: the essence of prayer, God's existence, the resurrection of the dead, the afterlife, the untimely death of children, and repentance.
Israel Costa used various sources, reformulating them and frequently making significant changes to them. This work analyzes each story by locating the source/s and the
changes made to them and offering an explanation for the divergence from the original
version. Little research has been conducted on Costa’s book, and the entire body of its
100 stories is analyzed here for the first time.
A statistical analysis of the 100 stories was conducted according to various variables,
such as the source of the stories, the period and the country in which they are set, the 235
protagonist's gender, reference to social class, reference to education, etc. Such statistical analysis is not common in similar studies and constitutes a methodological innovation in the analysis of readers used in schools.
The stories revolve around two axes: the human axis (emphasizing values of justice,
equality, kindness, learning, and education) and the Jewish axis (preserving one’s Jewish identity, adherence to the Jewish-Sephardic tradition – recognizing the inalienable
virtues of Judaism, and mastering secular subjects, such as medicine, foreign languages,
philosophy, and astronomy).
The work finds that the anthology is concerned primarily in conveying didactic messages to its young readers, whereas the purpose of endowing the Hebrew Language is
secondary.
The work analyzes the didactic messages conveyed by the anthology against the backdrop of the processes of secularization and integration that the Italian Jews underwent
in the mid-nineteenth century. Costa sought to show his young readers that they could
integrate into Italian society and become loyal citizens and patriots of the Italian homeland on the one hand, and on the other hand continue to preserve their Jewish identity
and Jewish culture.
The stories in the anthology imply that harsh decrees and hatred toward the Jews belong
to the past, and that with the onset of modernity the Gentiles no longer wished that Jews
would convert. On the contrary, any attempt by the Jews to convert or alienate themselves from their Jewish identity was met by fierce criticism on the part the Gentiles,
who wished to see the Jews integrating into Italian society while preserving their religion and culture.
This theme fits the overall orientation of the reader: presenting an idyllic state of affairs
free of moral and value dilemmas, in which every story has a happy ending and the
sinners mend their ways or repent their evil deeds. 236

Preface
The anthology Mikveh Israel (Livorno 1851) by Rabbi Israel Costa (1819-1897) is one
of the first anthologies for children written in Hebrew in the nineteenth century. An
important clarification should be noted here: While Costa's book is considered an anthology, this classification is not accurate. The typical anthology compiles several texts
from various sources, either retaining their original wording or paraphrasing them. In
Mikveh Israel, Costa generally drew from several sources, but in each case he processed
and restated the source, sometimes in a biased and selective manner. It appears that
Costa chose to “doctor” his sources in order to convey certain messages to his young
readers.
The meaning of the title of the anthology, Mikveh Israel, is "The Hope of Israel,” cited
from Jeremiah 14:8 ("Hope of Israel, its Rescuer in time of disasters"). All the biblical
quotations in this work are from the Hebrew Bible: A Translation with Commentary by
Robert Alter.
The title also refers to the author's given name, as do the titles of his other books:
.1853 _ "; "ישיר ישראל1890 _ ""כי נער ישראל
(Menashe ben Israel wrote a book with the same title, which appeared in 1650.)
In the first section of my work I do the following: First, I divide the 100 stories of the
anthology into seven content groups, and then I analyze each story, comparing it to its
source or sources. Locating the sources of the stories often involved considerable detective work.
In the second section I present a statistical analysis of the 100 stories based on various
variables.
The third section of my work is devoted to discussion and conclusions.
Introduction
Costa's anthology sought to instill in its young readers values that can be placed along
two axes: the first axis contains fundamental universal humanist values: telling the 237
truth, the importance of learning and education, helping others, family values (respecting one’s parents and the importance of family ties), diligence, and keeping a tidy notebook.
The values on the second axis serve to reinforce Jewish identity and adherence to Jewish culture among boys and girls who were raised within a minority group in an Italian
society that was beginning to offer emancipation to the Jews who sought to integrate in
it. As we shall see, Costa encouraged the Jews to integrate in the evolving Italian nationstate, while maintaining their traditional Jewish culture and values.
Rabbi Piperno of Livorno, who was Costa's teacher and edited the anthology, wrote an
introduction to it in which he clearly laid out its purpose: "Every rabbi in every generation, when he saw his community going astray from the TORAH AND MITZVOT,
would guide them along right paths with bands of love to their heavenly father." In
Piperno's view, the root of the problem lay in the fact that the holy books were inaccessible to young people, since they could not read Hebrew. On the other hand, young
people were drawn to books written in their native Italian language. This inevitably led
to them "deserting the cheerfulness of the book of religion and its mitzvot."
Piperno thus believed that the anthology should primarily serve to draw the youth back
to the Jewish religion and that the aim of teaching them Hebrew was secondary.
From the abovementioned introduction we see a picture of a Jewish community that is
moving away from Judaism and from observance of the Mitzvot. Five years previously,
Piperno described in more extreme language the drift away from religion: "…the faith
is decreasing and EPICORSSOUT (heresy) and lawlessness are increasing in the country." – KOL 'UGAV (1846).
In their introduction to the Hebrew translation of the book ELIEZER et NEPHTALY by
Jean-Pierre Claris de Florian (1853), Fiorentino and Costa express fear of the disappearance of the Jewish people from history: "We will always be remembered, and we
will not be like other previous people, the Amorites, Perizzities, Hitites and Jebusites
who have disappeared forever."
They furthermore believed that the Jews of Italy and other countries were involved in
Gentile society and were influenced by its culture: 238
"How are we known to one another, as brothers we are of a heavenly father…whether
in our different ways of living from every nation? …and since the day we were mixed
with gentiles, we learned their deeds and we followed their ways…How could Israel
not learn their practices, trade with them, and buy bread and drink from them? ...and
fear that should he not socialize with them, their hate and animosity will grow?"
Interestingly, this was also the impression gained by Chaim Weizmann from his visit
to Italy in 1921: "Jewish emancipation in Italy has been complete since generations.
The congregation was small, but its members took an active part in Italian life – political
and economic, artistic and scientific and in all their dealings and their belongings they
were indistinguishable from other citizens, except for one thing – that they went to the
synagogue and not to the church. In Italy there are about 50,000 [Jews] in a population
of about forty million". (Weizmann, 1949).
I cite Weizmann here because his observation agrees with the entrenched conception
about the smoothness of the emancipation of the Jews of Italy.
Michele Luzzati wrote as follows about the Jews of Italy in the nineteenth century:
"With the passing of time a secularization process took place among most Italian Jews
to the point of alienation from religious observance, and only a small number continued
to maintain a religious life-style as before." – Michele Luzzatti. "Italy and Its Jews." in
Roni Weinstein (ed.). Italy, 2012, p. 17 (in Hebrew).
A certain letter which was written in the 1870s and sent from Italy to the USA, described the situation of the Jews of Livorno as follows: "As far as religion is concerned,
it has completely disappeared. The families that are still religious are quite few." (Alessandro Guetta: 2009, p. 215 n. 25.)
Schachter came to the same conclusion:
"… Erosion of the traditional bonds that bound the individual Jew to his community
and the abandonment of religious practices, leading, in some cases, to mixed marriage
and conversion." (Schachter: 2011, p. 4.)
Costa was undoubtedly aware of the extent of conversion of Jews in Italy. He composed
a song of praise to Eliyahu Benamozegh, who dissuaded a Jew from converting. 239
It is appropriate to add a note of caution here. Two historians of nineteenth century
Italian Jewry informed me that the state of secularization of Italian Jews that I described
for the year 1851 in fact materialized only at least a decade later and gathered pace in
the subsequent decades. I suppose that they are right. Nevertheless, the rabbis Piperno
and Costa felt that the process of secularization in 1846-1853 was already in full swing,
as I have shown above by quoting them. They were no doubt expressing their subjective
feeling about the matter and thus perhaps exaggerated somewhat the gray reality. In
any case, their prognosis regarding the secularization process turned out to be accurate.
Therefore, Costa felt an urgent need to act to halt the progress of secularization and he
believed that his anthology could have the desired effect. Both Costa and Piperno believed that educational messages conveyed through stories such as those in the anthology Mikveh Israel could help achieve this goal. Second, they believed that by acquiring
a command of the Hebrew knowledge, their pupils would be drawn to the great works
of Jewish religion and literature. They also thought that a knowledge of Hebrew would
strengthen their pupils’ Jewish identity and contribute to their sense of belonging to the
Jewish people.
Thus, the main purpose of the anthology is educational. It is designed to educate a new
generation of Jews who would live in an open Italian society. Costa was aware of the
dangers that such a society posed to the continuation of Jewish life, and he sought to
confront these dangers in his anthology.
How did Costa perceive the place of the Jews in Italian society, which had begun to
open its gates to them? We find an indirect answer to this thorny question in his anthology. Furthermore, there is an additional source in which he explicitly depicts the status
of the Jews of Italy.
The source is a poem he wrote when the Grand Duke of Tuscany declared in the year
1848 that the Jews would be granted equal rights:
"The time of love has come…
The king has decreed one law in all Tuscany…
We shall rush to take up arms to be among the brave…
We shall fight against the enemies of Italy… 240
Therefore, we shall proclaim our joy because in her [Italy]
We have a share
As a mother good to us, we are her sons."
Israel Costa:1890 .כי נער ישראל. pp. 52-53.
Costa's declarations on the willingness of the Jews to die for Italy were tested in the
struggles and battles that took place during the Risorgimento, in which many Jews were
killed, in larger numbers than their proportion in the population. (Cecil Roth: 1946,
pp. 454-455.)
Costa's patriotic orientation toward Italy was not unusual among his contemporary Italian rabbis. Elizabeth Schachter argues that the rabbis played an important role in shaping the civic and patriotic consciousness of the Jews of Italy, both as teachers in the
education system and in their sermons in synagogues. (Schachter: 2011, pp. 16, 77).
Carlotta Ferrara wrote as follows about the symbolic significance of Jews' participation
in the Risorgimento: "…those who died in the battles of the Risorgimento acquired the
status of martyrs who had given their lives for a double cause: the defense of their
fatherland, and the demonstration of bravery and patriotism to their fellow citizens."
(2017, p. 170.)
The challenges that Costa confronted in his anthology are the same as those that Italian
Jews faced a few years later:
"Immediately after being granted equality, individual Jews, Jewish communities and
their leaders found themselves facing various challenges. They now had opportunities
for integration …and they experienced both euphoria and that they should demonstrate
…loyalty to state and fatherland. …This leads to the other challenge faced by the Jewish elites…; they had to combat the danger of gradual assimilation into the majority
society, aided by increasing secularization, the disappearance of the Jews themselves."
(Ferrara degli Uberti: 2017, pp. 4-5).
As I demonstrate in what follows, certain issues that surfaced in the Jewish discourse
in the years following the publication of Mikveh Israel (such as patriotism and fighting
for the fatherland, and recalling the bravery of the Maccabees) already appeared in Costa's anthology, although not always subject to the same interpretation. 241
The modern Jewish national awakening through the Zionist movement among the Jews
of Italy would appear only decades latter.
See the analysis of Zionism in Italy:
•
Schachter: 2011, pp. 165-194, 199-205.
•
Carlotta Ferrara degli Uberti: 2017, pp. 182-195, 218-224.
Like almost as all the rabbis of Italy, Costa was not influenced by Rabbi Dr Yehuda
Leon Bibas (1789-1852), a precursor of Zionism. On this interesting figure, who
was raised in Livorno, see:
Weiler-Israel, Yael. "Rabbi Dr Yehuda Aryeh Leon Bibas precursor of Zionism."
"Time for Pity". In Asaf Yedidya (ed.). 2015, pp. 50-69 (in Hebrew).
The Manuscript
The manuscript of the anthology survived and is kept in the archive of the synagogue
of Livorno. It is not punctuated. (I studied this manuscript in Livorno for several hours).
A microfilm of the manuscript can be accessed in the national library in Jerusalem (no.
148). I did not undertake a systematic and comprehensive comparison between the
printed book and the manuscript. I checked the manuscript in order to detect whether
certain mistakes were a printer’s error or appeared in the original manuscript.
During my visit to the archive of the synagogue in March 2017, I was told that all the
material pertaining to Costa in the archive was destroyed along with the synagogue
building by Allied bombers in 1944.
Part I – The Analysis of the Stories
I divided the stories into seven groups according to their content:
A. Biographies of Jewish personalities – 11 stories
B. Exemplary figures of Jews and non-Jews – 11 stories
C. Stories designed to instill virtues in children – 23 stories
D. Stories from the lives of children in the family, in school, and in peer groups
– 17 stories 242
E. Stories that show that Jews throughout history observed their religion in the
face of edicts by foreign rulers and were willing to die for Kiddush Hashem
(endure martyrdom) – 10 stories
F. Stories that show that gentiles were not impressed by Jews who converted or
tried to assimilate and commended Jews who preserved their Jewish or religious
identity – 8 stories.
G. Stories that represent the Jewish religion through its beliefs and positions, emphasize
the centrality of prayer, and address theological issues – 20 stories.
The theological issues addressed are: the essence of prayer, God's existence, the resurrection of the dead, the afterlife, the untimely death of children, and repentance.
In part I, I analyze three aspects of each story. First, I make a comparison between the
source of the story and the story as phrased by Costa, and seek to explain why Costa
sometimes made crucial changes to his sources. Second, I refer to background material
and in some cases offer an additional interpretation of the story, which does not always
agree with Costa's interpretation. Third, I try to explain his linguistic choices. He evidently made these choices intentionally, in order to suggest an alternative or a parallel
to other stories in the Bible, and thereby to offer additional meanings to the original
story.
I present here an analysis of two stories: story no. 86, which belongs to group E, and
story no. 23, which belongs to group F, as examples of part I of my study.
Story no. 86
Costa here exemplifies the tragedy of the expulsion from Spain through the personal
story of a man named Menashe. He employed a story that appears in Shlomo ibn
Verga's (1460-1554) book Sefer Shevet Yehudah, written in 1512 and published in
1550. (Ibn Verga was a historian and physician, and one of the Jews expelled from
Spain). The book describes the disasters that befell the Jewish people throughout history. Shevet= שבטin Hebrew means a rod used for corporal punishment, following
Lamentations, 3:1: "I am the man who has seen affliction by the rod of His wrath."
Yehudah refers to the author's first name but also to the Jews in general, the tribe of
Judah. 243
The book was republished by the Bialik Institute in 1947, with an introduction by
Yitzhak Baer and with detailed notes by Azriel Shochat.
This is the story told in Ibn Verga’s book : "I heard from old people from Spain, that a
ship was stricken by a plague, and the ship’s owner tossed them onto a deserted tract of
land and most of them died of starvation, and some of them tried to find a settlement.
And one Jew among them, he and his wife and two sons struggled to keep walking, and
his wife fainted and died, and he and his two sons fainted from hunger, and when he
awoke he found his two sons dead. And with concern he stood up and said: Master of
the Universe! You do much to cause me to leave my religion; know faithfully that at
the behest of the inhabitants of heaven I am a Jew and I will be a Jew and everything
you have brought upon me will not matter! And he gathered from the dirt and from the
weeds and covered the boys and went to seek for a settlement." p. 122.
In the original story, the hero is anonymous, and it was Costa who gave him the name
Menashe. This name alludes to the reason Joseph specified for naming his eldest son:
"And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, meaning, God has released me
from all the debt of my hardship, and of all my father's house." (Genesis 41, 51). While
Joseph forgot his past grief, here Menashe – representing the exiles from Spain – has
been forgotten by God. (It is interesting that the name of Agnon's tragic hero in And the
Crooked Shall Be Made Straight is also Menashe).
As is well known, the Jews of Spain who refused to convert to Christianity were forced
to leave the country. Costa estimates that the number of the expelled was 800,000; Don
Isaac Abravanel puts their number at 300,000; Gedaliah Ibn Yahya, author of Chain of
Kabbalah at 600,000; Spanish historian Jeronimo de Zurita y Castro referred to
400,000, and Juan de Mariana estimated the number could have reached 800,000. Contemporary scholars estimate a range of 100,000 to 200,000 (Wikipedia). Costa thus
apparently exaggerated the number of the expelled to enhance the colossal disaster that
befell the people of Israel.
Costa's linguistic choices are interesting. Referring to the Jews expelled from Spain he
writes: "and they went back and forth to find resting place for their feet." The allusion 244
is clear: the dove that Noah sent from the ark "found no resting place for its foot" (Genesis 8, 9). In other words, Costa suggests that the disaster is of the magnitude of the
Flood.
In describing the plot of the tale of Menashe and his family at sea, Costa alludes to the
book of Jonah: "Menashe...found a ship coming from Africa and he paid its fare and
went down into it." The book of Jonah 1:3 reads: “ And Jonah got up...and found a ship
coming from Tarshish, and he paid its fare and went down with them."
In Costa's version: "And there was a great storm on the sea, and the ship threatened to
break up. …...The captain brought Menashe and his family ashore to lighten the number of passengers on the ship." The book of Jonah 1: 4-15 reads: "And the LORD cast
a great wind upon the sea, and there was a great storm on the sea, and the ship threatened to break up. And the sailors were afraid…and they cast the gear that was in the
ship into the sea to lighten their load… And they lifted up Jonah, and cast him into the
sea, and the sea ceased from its fury."
The allusion to Jonah is by way of opposition. Jonah ran away voluntarily and sailed to
Tarshish, whereas Menashe and his family were expelled from Spain against their will.
In the book of Jonah, the captain casts objects into the sea in the face of the storm and
only when this is ineffective does he throw Jonah into the sea at his request. Whereas
in Costa’s story, the captain took Menashe and his family off the ship and abandoned
them on a deserted beach after the sea calmed down in order to lighten the ship and to
usurp Menashe’s property.
There is a further connection between Jonah and Menashe. Just as Jonah could not escape his destiny, so Menashe cannot escape his Jewishness, nor does he wish to. It is
true that he was born a Jew – which was beyond his control – but he chose to remain a
Jew, even though this put his life at risk.
In Costa’s story we also find a contrast to Psalms 107: 4-6, which glorifies God as the
savior of people who find themselves in distress. For example, the poet there describes
people who "wandered in wilderness…hungry, thirsty, too, their life-breath failed
within them. And they cried to the LORD in their straits, from their distress He saved
them". Whereas Menashe and his family were deserted on a shore, hungry and thirsty, 245
praying to God for help, but their prayer was not answered. Menashe, like Job, lost his
family and his property.
At the end of the story Menashe turns to God. He attributes his adherence to God to the
catastrophes that befell him following the expulsion. Had he agreed to become a Christian, he could have saved his family and his property, but he refused and chose to endure
expulsion. In his address to God, Menasheh says: "Even if you come back to me and
turn Your hand against me all day, I will not complain about you." Costa made use of
the verse from Lamentations 3:3: "Just to me He comes back, turns His hand against
me all day." In doing so, he likens the magnitude of the disaster of the expulsion from
Spain to the destruction of the First Temple. As is well known, the expulsion order
directed at Jews who did not convert to Christianity set the final date of Tisha B'Av (the
ninth day of Av) for leaving Spain. More precisely, the date was AV the seventh, but
in the historical memory the expulsion from Spain was linked to Tisha B'Av, along with
other disasters that befell the Jewish people, such as the destruction of the First and
Second Temples.
Menashe steadfastly adheres to his belief in God and declares: "I was born a Jew and
a Jew I will die." In the aforementioned source the wording is: "I am a Jew and I will
be a Jew." Menashe's statement, according to Costa, is slightly different from that in
the original. It is possible that Costa hints at Menashe's willingness to die for Kiddush
Hashem.
Megillat [scroll] Amraphel was written by the Kabbalist Abraham ben Eliezer Halevi
(1460 –1530-1535). The Megilla is intended to guide those who wish to die as martyrs
how to moderate their excruciating suffering. It recommends, for example: "…for one
who is resolved to sanctify the name of God when they torture him excessively and
implore and demand of him, saying that if he relinquishes his faith they will leave him
and cause him no pain, or in a case where he must inform them of his decision…he
should answer thus: ‘I am a Jew and I shall remain a Jew and I shall die a Jew.’ He
should be resolved to sanctify his creator and not to desecrate the name of God. And
such a one will not feel the tortures that they inflict upon him."
In Megillat Amraphel the believer declares that he is willing to die for his faith. In
Costa’s story Menashe likewise declares: "I was born a Jew and a Jew I will die,"
thereby indicating a willingness to die for Kiddush Hashem. 246
It should be noted that Gershom Scholem, who first published "Megillat Amraphel,"
believed that Abraham Halevi was referring to the Inquisition, which operated during
that time in Spain (Episodes from the History of Kabbalah Literature. Kiryat Sefer,
seventh year 1930-1931, pp.152-155). Abraham Gross disagreed with him and suggested a different thesis. See: "The Ashkenazi Syndrome of Martyrdom in Portugal in
1497," especially the appendix: "The Historical Background of Megillat Amraphel.”
Tarbitz 64, A, 1995. pp. 108-114.
Interestingly, a similar statement was made by Solika Hachuel (1817-1834), a Moroccan Jewess who was executed for alleged apostasy. She was accused of abandoning the
religion of Islam after she converted to it. One who revokes his or her conversion to
Islam is called in Arabic an apostate ( )مرتدand the penalty is death. Just before she was
executed, she declared: "I was born a Jew and I die a Jew." (Dan Ben Amos et al:
2006, pp. 87-94.)
Many Americans are familiar with a similar statement made by a famous American
regarding his unconditional loyalty to his country. I am referring to the statement of
senator and statesman Daniel Webster (1782-1852), who pronounced:
"I was born an American; I will live an American; I shall die an American." (Webster, 1850, p. 15).
It is notable that Harvard Law Professor Alan Dershowitz declared in his opening remarks in memory of the Jewish journalist Daniel Pearl, who was executed by extremists
in Pakistan:
"I am a Jew. I was born a Jew. I have lived my life as a Jew. And I will die a Jew."
See:
Alan Dershowitz, in: I am Jewish: Personal Reflections Inspired by the Last Words of
Daniel Pearl. Edited by Judea and Ruth Pearl. 2004, p. 117.
While Dershowitz's statement is very Jewish, it is at the same time a patriotic American
pronouncement, because it alludes to Daniel Webster's statement.
Chaim Raphael (1924-2014), a Sephardi Jew who was born in Thessaloniki and was
the only member of his family to survive Auschwitz, said in an interview with Yad 247
Vashem: "We were a big family, everybody was sent to the crematorium and I remained alone… I was born a Jew; it is impossible to escape it ... I was born a Jew and
I will die a Jew with pride."
The statement is intended to convey the following message: I had no choice as to which
nation to be born into. But the decision to retain this identity attests to my voluntary
choice to belong to this nation, even if it involves paying a heavy price.
I mentioned cases in which Jews declared their loyalty to their Jewish identity at the
risk of death, centuries after 1492 up until the twentieth century. This goes to show that
Costa was wrong in thinking that this declaration belonged to the bygone history of the
Jewish people.
Finally, I wish to address the final sentence of the story: "Pity me God and in the shadow
of your wings I will take refuge." The phrase 'to take refuge under wings' appears twice
in the Bible and the wings are the wings of God:
A. The Book of Ruth 2:12 – Boaz praised Ruth, who converted to Judaism: "May The
LORD requite your actions and may your reward be complete from the Lord God of
Israel under Whose wings you have come to shelter". Menashe, on the other hand, suffered because he insisted on remaining a Jew.
B. In Psalms 91:4 it is said: "With His pinion He shelters you, and beneath His wings
you take refuge". This chapter is recited, inter alia, during funerals and Menashe may
have uttered it while burying his wife and sons. Yet he uses the above sentence in praying and in the hope that God would save him from imminent death.
Story no. 23
To the coachman's surprise, the Christian clergyman – Cheverus – commands him to
increase the donation to the poor woman when he learned that she was Jewish. His
reasoning was this: he knows that his coreligionists will not give alms to a poor Jew
and therefore he gave her a generous gift.
The message: not all Christians are hostile to us and some of them are among the Righteous Among the Nations who go out of their way to treat the Jews well. 248
In medieval Jewish literature the term 'Righteous Among the Nations' denotes a gentile
who observes the Seven Laws of Noah, for example: not to worship idols, and not to
commit murder or incest. (See for example: Maimonides. Mishneh Torah. The Laws of
Kings and Their Wars. 8, 11. The term was used before him by Midrash Agur, circa
800 AD.)
In modern times, the term denotes a gentile who displays an extraordinarily positive
attitude toward Jews. Costa was among the first to use this term in its modern sense.
After the Holocaust, the Righteous Among Nations are non-Jews who risked their lives
to save Jews during the Holocaust and were recognized as such by Yad Vashem.
The concluding sentence of the story – "In my opinion and in the opinion of my coreligionists" – corresponds to the preamble of the story, which indicates that the benefactor is a Christian clergyman. (In the Letter of James 2:1 he addresses his audience as
"brothers in faith": "My brothers, show no partiality as you adhere to the faith in our
glorious Lord Jesus Christ").
This statement did not appear in the source of the story. Costa’s addition implies that
in his act Cheverus represents all Christians, a conclusion negated by the words of his
servant, who objected to the giving of alms to the poor Jew. Perhaps this explains why
Costa turned his companion into a lowly servant, whereas in the 1838 source of the
story his companion was a priest (aumonier=chaplain).
Who is Cheverus in this story? He is Jean Louis Lefebvre de Cheverus (1768-1836),
who served as bishop of Boston, and who at the end of his life, from 1826 to1836,
served as archbishop of Bordeaux, France. He maintained cordial relations with the
Jews of the city, most of whom originated from Spain and Portugal. It is said that the
rabbi of Bordeaux made a point of maintaining ongoing contact with Cheverus and
complimented him at their first encounter on his wisdom, comparing it to the wisdom
of Solomon. When the rabbi's daughter died, Cheverus expressed his pain and sorrow,
saying to him: "I come to find solace from the representative of the Christian Jesus, who
cried over Lazarus' tomb." The author of the book took the words of the rabbi as proof
that the unbelieving Jews cherished him. (Andre Jean Marie Hamon: 1841, pp. 337338. 249
This book was translated into English two years later, because Cheverus had served as
bishop of Boston. (J. Huen Dubourg (pseudonym for Andre Jean Marie Hamon): 1839,
p. 270.)
This story – no. 23 – appears in two books in slightly different versions:
L'Abbe P.P: 1838, p. 114.
The second book was published in the United States in 1982:
John O'Kane Murray: 1882, pp. 376-381.
The 1838 source relates the story as a testament to the tolerance of Cheverus, probably
given the unusual way he treated a poor Jewess, all the more so in the face of the reservations of his companion (who was a priest, rather than a coachman, as Costa portrayed
him) for giving alms to a Jewish woman. The tolerance Cheverus displayed is also reflected in the cordial relations he built with Protestants in Boston, where he served as a
bishop from 1808 to 1823, and with Protestants in Montauban, France, where he served
as bishop from 1823 to 1826. The story in the 1882 source appears following a reference
to Cheverus’ positive attitude toward Protestants in Boston.
It is interesting to note that the same story is attributed in a different book to Charles
Francois d'Aviau Du Bois de Sanzay (1736 - 1826), who preceded Cheverus in office. It
is brought as an example of generosity. This bishop likewise maintained relatively good
relations with the Jews of Bordeaux. (Emile Gigault de la Bedolliere: 1850, p. 286.)
This title is reminiscent of the sentence that appears in the title of Mikveh Israel: "And
it is a moral book to educate the boys." It is quite possible that this book, along with
many others published at that time in France that shared the same purpose, motivated
Costa to compose his book. Drori (2018) expresses the same idea.
This story also appears in the biography on Bishop de Sanzay. I bring this additional
source for the following reason: The author of that biography claims that the bishop
gave alms to all poor people regardless of religious affiliation, be it Jewish, Lutheran,
Calvinist, Quaker, or Methodist; or their nationality, be it French, Spanish, Italian, Mexican, Canadian, or Chinese. Following the story about giving alms to the poor Jewess,
the biographer adds that this act constitutes an appropriate response to all allegations of
intolerance "that our enemies attribute to us." As mentioned above, the 1838 source on 250
Cheverus likewise claims that his generosity towards the poor Jewess was indicative of
his tolerance.
Details of the biography: Jean Paul Francois Marie Lyonnet: 1847, pp. 616-617.
Costa tells the story about Cheverus to show that Christians were sympathetic toward
Jews, while the additional source interprets the act of the bishop as proof that he gave
alms to all people in need, regardless of their religion or nationality, and not as an expression of love for Jews or a desire to treat them particularly well. Costa, hence, did
not only at times alter the facts that appeared in his sources, but also offered a different
interpretation of the sources. To illustrate this conclusion, let us address the second
version of the story about the Bishop of Bordeaux, who preceded Cheverus. The source
from 1838 brought the story to demonstrate Cheverus' overall tolerance rather than his
particular love of the Jews.
I believe that the story attributed to Cheverus was true, while the story attributed to his
predecessor in Bordeaux is an invention. This is because the story about Cheverus appeared in writing in 1838, two years after his death, while the story about his predecessor appeared first in 1847, 21 years after his death. Since he served in the same position
in Bordeaux as Cheverus and was also sympathetically inclined toward the Jews, people
attributed the story to him as well. (One may reach the opposite conclusion, or conclude that the story is true of both the bishops.) The different sources actually tell the
same story, but there are differences between them in terms of the following details:
the identity of the generous bishop, the place where the act took place, the amount donated, the gender of the recipient of the alms, the identity of the companion, and so
forth. This is typical of folk tales that are passed down by word of mouth.
In any case, the reader who is unfamiliar with Cheverus' positive attitude toward the
Jews has some difficulty in linking his exalted title as a Righteous Among the Nations
given to him by Costa, with his rather modest gesture toward the poor Jewess.
Yet another similar story is to be found. Pope Pius IX, who served as pope from1846
to 1878, saw on one of his trips a sick old man at the side of the road, not far from the
ghetto. When asked, the coachman answered that the old man was a Jew. The pope
responded: "And is he not a human being, whom we should help?" He stopped the car- 251
riage, drove the sick old Jewish man to his house, and stayed with him until he recovered. The incident occurred in 1846. (The story resembles the parable of "The Good
Samaritan"). The source: Hulskamp, Franz, Wilhelm Molitor: 1875. p. 93.
Pius IX was involved in the affair of Edgardo Mortara. See below on p. 263.
Costa was probably familiar with the 1838 source but he made changes to it, as he often
did. First, he turned the alms from silver into gold. Second, he mentions that the incident took place near Cheverus' carriage, whereas it was originally stated that it took
place as he left the church. Moreover, the companion was a coachman, based on the
above story about Pope Pius IX and the ill Jew he encountered while travelling in his
carriage.
A note: the anthology Mikveh Israel is available online on the site of the National Library in Jerusalem.
Part II – Statistical Analysis of the Stories
I conducted a statistical analysis of the stories. Each story was considered as one record
in a file of 100 records. The absolute numbers also represent percentages, as there are
100 records (stories).
The variables of the records I analyzed are as follows: the length of the story; the source
of the story; the period in history in which the story is set; the country in which the story
occurred; the gender of the protagonist in the story; the age of the protagonist; the identity of the protagonist: Jew/non-Jew; identifiable historical figures in the story; the surroundings within which the story occurred: family, school, community, state (kingdom), and royal court; the subjects of the stories; positive reference to learning and
education; reference to the protagonist’s social class (poor or rich); the social status of
the characters in the story; literary genre: parables and lessons.
I present here a statistical analysis of only four variables: the source of the story, the
country in which the story is set, reference to the poor and the rich, and positive references to learning and education. 252
The Source of the Story
The distribution of the stories by literary source:
The Bible – 4 stories
Historical sources – 21 stories
Chazal, Apocrypha, Josephus and others – 29 stories
Folk stories and legends – 18 stories
Costa’s first-hand knowledge or stories that he composed – 28 stories.
The Country in which the Story Occurred
Italy – 34 stories
Eretz Israel – 26 stories
France – 12 stories
Spain + Portugal – 7 (Spain – 6, Portugal – 1)
Germany – 5
Other Countries – 7
Unknown – 9.
It should be noted that all the stories that Costa himself composed (those without a
source) are set in Italy. If we exclude Eretz Israel, most of the stories are set in Western
countries: Italy, France, Spain and Germany. One should remember that ties existed
between the Jews of Italy and the Jews of France and of Germany.
It is interesting to note that there is almost no reference in the anthology to Jews who
live in Muslim countries, even though 16 percent of all Jews lived in Asia and Africa
at the time.
Costa’s disregard of the Jews who lived in Eastern Europe, 70% of the Jewish population of the world, is even more striking. 253
Sergio Della Pergola. "Some Fundamentals of Jewish Demographic History." In S.
Della Pergola, J. Evens (eds.). Papers in Jewish Demography 1997. Jerusalem: The
Hebrew University, 2001. (The data refer to 1825). See Part III; Discussion and Conclusions.
Reference to the Poor and the Rich
Reference to social class is very prevalent in the anthology. Thirty-one stories refer to
the poor; 24 refer to the rich; and 20 stories deal with both the poor and the rich. Eleven
stories refer exclusively to the poor, while four stories refer exclusively to the rich. In
total, we find 35 stories that refer to the poor and/or to the rich.
The frequent reference to the dichotomy between the poor and the rich is indicative of
the dual conception that Costa had of his own society and of the gaps between the two
groups. The data show that poverty was a common phenomenon in the Italy of his generation.
Canepa notes that prior to the emancipation and for many years thereafter the poor
constituted a substantial stratum of almost every Jewish community, and charitable
bodies were established to assist them. In Livorno of 1846, for example, there were 70
welfare institutions in a community of approximately 5,000 people.
Andrew M. Canepa. "Emancipation and Jewish Response in Mid-Nineteenth Century
Italy." European History Quarterly. 1986, 16, 4. pp. 403-439.
In 1844, 19 private educational institutions operated in Livorno, in addition to the local
community Talmud Torah. Elizabet Schachter, 2011, pp. 77, 93 n83 (based on Liana
Funaro and Carlotta Ferrara degli Uberti).
The Jewish community's schools served mostly the poor throughout Italy: "Many Jewish families chose to send their children to public schools, especially among the more
established economic classes, while poor families were forced to send their children to
"assisted and philanthropic" schools within the Jewish community. This was because
Jewish schools handed out generous cash prizes for academic achievement or pupil
attendance, and even granted subsidies to families so that they would send their children
to school instead of going off to work." Sylvia Guetta. "Education." In Roni Weinstein
(editor). Italy. 2012, p. 68 (in Hebrew). 254
Abraham Berliner, who visited Italy for six months in 1873, wrote as follows about his
visit to Livorno: "Jews participate in all public affairs and they contribute more than
their fair share in promoting and developing public affairs. Yet they still equipped their
institutions well, in the same manner that they cared for their poor, who existed in great
numbers in their community side by side with the extremely rich." Abraham Berliner. Six Months in Italy. 1945, p. 51 (in Hebrew).
Costa himself taught in the community’s education system designed for indigent pupils. There were also many private schools with Jewish teachers, including some operated by women for pupils from higher class families (Liana Funaro – personal communication). Costa himself came from a low economic class (Drori, 2018, p. 57, note
6).
Gadi Luzzatto-Voghera claims that from the second half of the eighteenth century the
rabbis of Italy generally belonged to the low or middle classes... “The rabbis were generally regarded as junior officials in the communities, who taught the foundations of
Judaism." Gadi Luzzato-Voghera. "Cultural and Religious Activity." in Roni Weinstein
(ed.). Italy. 2012. p. 91 (in Hebrew).
The education system of the community in Livorno was called Pie Scuole.
Against this backdrop it is instructive to read some of the stories that deal with poor
pupils. In one of the stories (no. 80) supervisors came to interview pupils concerning
work. It is likely that poor pupils went to work at a young age. The type of work they
did does not seem to have required considerable cerebral skills, since the supervisors
preferred to employ the less smart pupil whose notebooks were tidy rather than a bright
pupil who did not keep his notebooks neat.
Story no. 31 tells of an orphan girl who took on the role of her parents as the provider
of the family.
Story no. 100 tells of Hillel, who, although he was a poor woodcutter, spent a considerable portion of his salary on acquiring an education. Costa understandably included a
story about Scheppler (no. 5), who initiated the opening of schools for the poor.
Costa clearly sought to instill in his pupils the realization that acquiring education
would help them find work and so support their family. 255
In two stories Costa glorifies poverty and finds benefits in it (14, 67).
Had we not known that there was a separate education system for poor pupils in Livorno
and that Costa taught there and might also have included his book Mikveh Israel in the
curriculum, we would not understand why he devoted so many stories to the poor and
the rich and why he found that poverty held certain advantages over wealth.
Positive Reference to Learning and Education
Learning constitutes a major activity of the anthology's protagonists, and Costa devoted
20 stories explicitly to commend learning and education.
Why, according to Costa, is it important to acquire education? There are two equally
important answers:
a. To acquire knowledge and the joy of learning.
b. Education is a means toward acquiring a profession and an income that would
contribute to the family's livelihood, help gain respect from one’s parents and
the community, and make parents and relatives happy.
An additional reason which is mentioned in a few cases is the contribution of education
to reinforcing religious belief and the observance of mitzvot.
The ideal of reciting the Torah day and night or the ideal of devoting oneself almost
exclusively to studying the Torah ("to kill yourself over the Torah") are not mentioned
in the anthology. 256
Part III – Discussion and Conclusions
Emancipation, Assimilation and Secularization
In 1848-1849 almost all the states of Italy declared Jews to be equal citizens. Jews had
begun to integrate in Italian society at the turn of the eighteenth century and this process
accelerated following the occupation of parts of Italy by Napoleon, leading to the beginning of secularization and a move away from religion.
In group F Costa emphasized to his pupils that not only did gentile society not encourage the assimilation of Jews, but it in fact looked askance at attempts made by Jews to
assimilate or to renounce their religion. Precisely because Costa believed that Italian
society welcomed Jews to integrate and did not discriminate them, he feared that this
would lead Jews to abandon their religion and their Jewish identity. Costa did not directly refer to the problems of assimilation and secularization. This is in line with his
tendency to present an optimistic and idyllic picture of the world.
The figures whose biographies Costa chose to relate are those that were rooted in religious Jewish culture but also mastered foreign languages and studied science and other
secular fields (philosophy, medicine, and astronomy). Some, like Josephus, Abravanel
and the Rothschilds, were commended by the elites of gentile societies.
Costa sought to impress upon his pupils that one could be both a good Jew and a good
Italian, and that one could be attached to both the Jewish and the general culture. It
should be noted that these trends were not new to Jewish Sephardi culture and to the
Jews of Italy. This trend culminated in the Golden Age in Spain and was sustained in
Italy by Spanish and Portuguese immigrants who arrived to its shores. Therefore, it is
not surprising that the modern movement of enlightenment in Germany did not impress
the Jews of Italy, as Bregoli notes:
"The Haskalah was a conscious ideology of reform and critical reaction to Jewish tradition, aiming at individual and communal improvement in order to promote greater
Jewish cultural integration in the larger society. The fact that the movement of Jewish
reform and integration did not develop in Livorno is not entirely surprising. 257
Livornese Jews, like other Jews in Italy, did not need to become maskilim to appreciate
the importance of general knowledge. The Italian and Sephardi Jewish educational tradition did not view the pursuit of ‘external sciences’ as being in opposition to the study
of Torah." (Francesca Bregoli: 2014, p. 7.)
Asher Salah argues in a similar vein: "The term Haskalah, which was coined in Germany as a translation of the term Aufklarung (enlightenment), was not appropriate to
the circumstances of Italian Jewry. First, in Italy there was no movement with a clear
ideology based on a structured plan of religious and political reform of Judaism…Second, the Jews of Italy…were very receptive to the surrounding culture." "The Enlightenment." In Roni Weinstein (ed.). Italy: 2012, pp. 133-142 (in Hebrew).
Interestingly, we find the same trend in the work of Leone Racah, who knew Costa, in
his book for children: Il Plutarco Israelita. Livorno. 1881. Alongside traditional figures
such as Hillel, Rabbi 'Akiva and Rashi, he addressed men who were involved in the
general culture in which they lived, such as Philo, Josephus Flavius, Maimonides, Abravanel, Menashe ben Israel, Spinoza, and Mendelssohn. He considered these figures to
be on a par with Dante, Petrarch, Michelangelo, and Galileo. I rely here on:
Carlotta Ferrara degli Uberti: 2017, pp. 174-175.
Some of the characters introduced by Racah were mentioned before him by Costa.
Some of them were Sephardim. Livorno was founded by Jews from Spain and Portugal
and in the mid-nineteenth century they still constituted a large majority among the Livornese Jews.
Hence, Costa’s Sephardi pupils could readily identify with these figures: "Although
there are stories about these figures in all Jewish communities, when they are told by
Spanish immigrants a sense of emotional closeness and group pride is created." Tamar
Alexander-Frizer. "Folk Creation." In Yaron ben Naeh (ed.). Turkey. 2012, pp. 107-122
(in Hebrew).
It is appropriate to note here that Costa frequently appended to his name the proud
initials Samech Teit – Sephardi Tahor, a pure Sephardi=ספרדי טהור ס"ט.
Costa chose stories set in Western and Central Europe but ignored those that dealt with
Jews of Muslim countries, for two reasons. First, these Jews were exposed to Western 258
culture only in 1862, with the founding of the Alliance Israelite Universelle educational
organization, which introduced the Enlightenment movement to Muslim countries
(North Africa and the Middle East, including Eretz Israel).
Second, Costa believed that the status of the Jews in Muslim countries was inferior and
that they were incapable of developing independent thinking.
While I have no evidence that this claim was valid in 1851, we find supporting evidence
27 years later, in the case of Nissim Samama's will. Costa was involved in an acerbic
dispute over the validity of the Tunisian Caid's will. He argued that the Tunisian rabbis
could not assume an independent standpoint because they did not live as free citizens
in a Muslim country and they feared the Tunisian authorities. Whereas the Jews of Italy,
as those in other Western European nations, enjoyed freedom and equality and could
voice their opinions freely, without fear. See Appendix II: The case of Nissim Samama's will.
In 1880 Costa wrote a book which includes stories and legends from Muslim countries:
Sefer 'Aravim Bebtokhah – in Hebrew: ספר ערב"ים בתוכה.
This book resembles Tales from a Thousand and One Nights. This may seem to suggest
that Costa did find interest in the Jews of Muslim countries. Yet this is not the case,
because he did not bring concrete stories of Jews in Muslim countries within historical
contexts, but rather regarded them as exotic literature from the Orient, which could not
teach us anything about the way of life or culture of the Jews in the lands of Ishmael.
In his anthology Costa likewise ignored the Jews of Russia and Poland, who constituted
70 percent of the Jewish people in the world. He did so because they were only in the
early stage of the Haskalah movement in 1851. Only later did it become a mass movement by virtue of the expansion of modern schools. By contrast, in the mid-nineteenth
century the Haskalah movement had already laid deep roots among the Jews of Western
Europe.
Costa relates a story about a Jewish soldier in Napoleon's army who was courageous in
battle, and about Alphonse Picard, a Jew who participated in the July 1830 revolution
and died for the French homeland. These stories were designed to show that Jews could 259
integrate into gentile society, where they were granted freedom and equality and became loyal sons of their homeland. Picard's willingness to die for his homeland – France
– proves his identification with it. Jews in the modern age have frequently offered similar arguments. Here is one example of many: Marc Bloch, the great French-Jewish
historian, wrote in 1940:
"I need to say no more in rebuttal of such a charge [that I am an 'alien'] than that my
great-grandfather was a serving soldier in 1793, that my father was one of the defenders
of Strasbourg in 1870." Strange Defeat. (Origin in French: L'Etrange Defaite).
Costa includes several stories in which Napoleon is mentioned. By telling these stories,
Costa expresses his affection for him. Napoleon conquered parts of Italy at the turn of
the eighteenth century, granted emancipation and equal rights to Jews and opened the
gates of the ghettos. (Primo Levi tells of Jews who named their sons Napoleon).
Following the French Revolution and the emancipation of the Jews in France, it became
an ideal state model for Costa. In a poem he wrote to commemorate "the revolution of
February 1848" in which the second republic was established, he lauded France as a
source of inspiration and wisdom for many nations:
"A country of grace and beauty…
And a source of all wisdom." 1890 . כי נער ישראל. p. 54.
When Napoleon III's army besieged Rome in 1849 in a bid to return it to the Pope after
being controlled by the Italian Republicans, Costa vented his disappointment with
France in a poem: "France that in you we hoped as a land of desire, why have you
become our enemy…Lord God alone knows that we loved you with a deep love."
1890 .כי נער ישראל. Livorno. p. 58.
Our knowledge of the process of secularization of Italian Jewry explains why Costa
included the stories of group E and group F in his anthology.
This also explains why Costa barely mentioned in his anthology practical mitzvot, such
as kashrut and Shabbat observance laws. The sources of stories no. 17 and 87 relate that
the Greeks sought to force the Jews to eat pork. Costa makes no mention of this, but 260
merely relates that the Greeks sought to force the Jews to abandon their religion. Perhaps he was apprehensive of arousing antagonism or embarrassment among his pupils,
some of whom no longer adhered to kashrut or observance of Shabbat, with all its prohibitions.
Here I must add a reservation. The genre of the anthology is folk literature, and therefore we do not expect to find in it details of mitzvot. In Bialik and Ravnistky's Sefer
Ha'aggadah we likewise find scant reference to mitzvot and their ramifications.
Costa believed that the trend toward integration into Italian society among Jews could
not be reversed, but at the same time he sought through his book to reinforce the Jewish
identity and Jewish culture of his young readers, to dissuade them from assimilating
into Italian society.
Group G includes stories that raise theological issues, such as the premature death of
young children, doubts about the existence of God, and resurrection. In story no. 38, a
man who expressed doubts about resurrection, one of the cardinal principles of the Jewish faith according to Maimonides, did so in the synagogue. This was tantamount to an
act of heresy, since it was performed in a public and holy place. This story reveals that
heresy had begun to take root among Livornese Jews.
Apologetic books on the Jewish religion have generally appeared at times of cultural
change and the erosion of traditional principles of the Jewish faith. By the same token,
the inclusion of stories verging on heresy in Costa's anthology should be similarly understood.
It seems to me that Costa hoped to disseminate among his young pupils his ideas regarding the possibility of integrating in Italian society and at the same time maintaining
one’s Jewish culture. The children would then persuade their parents to accept this fundamental idea. I found a clue to this idea in the third story, where it is understated. The
child succeeds in persuading his father, a soldier, to begin to pray. A soldier is more
prone to lose his Jewish identity because he is no longer under the traditional wings and
control of the Jewish community. (Costa therefore places this story at the beginning of
his anthology.)
The idea of introducing cultural change through the education of children is not
farfetched. The great cultural transformation of North African Jews toward adopting 261
French culture was implemented through the Alliance educational system. (Perhaps it
is apt to mention here the saying of Ephraim Kishon: Israel is the only country in the
world where mothers learn their mother tongue from their children.)
Israelita
In the story about the brave acrobat Plege (no. 30), Costa called him a man of Israel.
(Jacob’s name was changed to Israel after his struggle with the angel. Genesis 32:29).
In the early nineteenth century the Jews of Italy began to use the term "Israelita". This
indicted that "The old Jew underwent rapid change due to emancipation and the process
of integration into the surrounding society, and also gained a new name: no longer
"ebreo" but "israelita" – son of Israel. The use of a new name was very widespread in
the second half of the nineteenth century," (Gadi Luzzatto Voghera. "Cultural and Religious Activity." In Roni Weinstein (ed.) Italy. 2012, p. 89 (in Hebrew).
Carlotta Ferrara pointed to similar trends toward changes in the terminology employed
by the Jews in France, the UK, and Germany. She argues that the term 'popolo ebraico'
was no longer compatible with the status of the Jews as citizens and members of the
evolving Italian nation, who were eager to discard the negative connotation that the
word “Jew” had borne for generations. She claims that the term “Israelita” was initially
used at the beginning of the nineteenth century and became widespread between 1820
and1830. Carlotta Ferrara: 2017, pp. 9-10.
The epithet "man of Israel" that Costa used for the acrobat defined him as a Jewish man
of a new breed.
Did Costa use the term "a man of Israel" to refer exclusively to Jews in the modern age?
Most definitely. Costa made a point of using the term to refer to Jews from 1800 onward, while up until then he used the traditional terms Jew, of the Sons of Israel, Israel,
and ebreo. In two stories soldiers who fought with Napoleon were called "a man of
Israel." The names Jew and ebreo are identical – in story no. 15 the physician was initially referred to as a Jew and thereafter as an ebreo.
This finding clearly demonstrates that Costa’s linguistic choices were not in the least
random, as I have shown throughout my work. 262
A Contradiction between Group E and Group F
I found a stark contradiction between two groups of stories: the stories in group E relate
attempts by Gentiles to force Jews to convert or to commit serious offenses (such as
idolatry). On the other hand, the stories in group F show that Gentiles disapproved of
attempts on the part of Jews to convert or to conceal their Jewish identity; on the contrary, Jews who adhered to their Jewishness were respected and commended by kings.
The most famous story of group F is no. 15. Francis I, the king of France, asked his
captor, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, to send a Jewish physician to cure him.
Charles V sent him a converted Jewish physician. Francis I refused to see him, claiming
that if he were indeed an expert physician he would not have abandoned his religion.
I suggest a partial reconciliation of the contradiction: the stories in the first group are
set in the ancient world (Greece and Rome), or in the Middle Ages up until the Spain
expulsion, whereas most of the stories in the second group are set the modern era.
Costa's message to his disciples was this: our ancestors were willing to forfeit their lives
to preserve their Jewishness. This is why we must continue to preserve our Judaism,
since assimilation merely impedes our advancement in gentile society. This argument
is flawed, since Jews gained advancement in Europe following their conversion and
some converted expressly for that purpose (for example, Karl Marx's father and Gustav
Mahler).
"There can be no doubt that the great majority of Jewish converts in the nineteenth century acted because of the legal and social conditions...Some converted in order to obtain
government and academic positions or in order to marry a Christian, others took this
step in order to enter into political life…They regarded conversion – as Heine put it –
as a ticket of admission to European society." (A History of the Jewish People. Edited
by H.H. Ben-Sasson. 1976, p. 826.)
Costa would not have agreed with the portrayal of Jewish history as presented in
Hazaz's story The Sermon. The protagonist of the story, Yudka, claims that the entire
course of Jewish history consists of exterminations, the abuse of Jews by Gentiles, and
pogroms: "What is it about?... Persecutions, massacres, martyrdoms and pogroms. And
more persecutions, persecutions, massacres, martyrdoms and pogroms." Hazaz: 2005,
p. 237. 263
Costa takes a different view: the persecutions belong to the past, and since the advent
of the modern era the attitudes of the Gentiles toward the Jews have changed for the
better.
Costa ignored the edicts and pogroms that had taken place in modern times . As to his
claim that Gentiles disapproved of Jews who had converted, he was plainly wrong.
First, there were gentiles in Western Europe who called upon Jews to assimilate into
their societies. On the other hand, paradoxically and contrary to expectations, Jews who
assimilated or converted were not always welcomed and their Jewishness was not forgotten by those who opposed the integration of the Jews into their society (as in the
case of Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy, for example).
Moreover, a new strand of anti-Semitism sprung up precisely against the backdrop of
Jews' assimilation. In the Middle Ages, Jews maintained their religious identity and
knew their place in Christian society. When they gained emancipation and assumed
positions in the fields of law, medicine, science, literature, economics, and finance, they
provoked antagonism and were perceived as threatening Western societies.
The second point is inconsistent with Costa's argument. He argues that the criticism of
Jews by gentiles stems from their positive attitude toward Jews and Judaism, and that
the Gentiles are willing to accept the Jews and integrate them into society while maintaining their Jewish identity. However, the negative attitudes displayed by reactionary
strata toward assimilators were rooted in their hatred of the Jews. They feared that the
penetration of Jews into gentile society would "pollute" it, and insisted that the Jews
remain in their own community on the margins of society.
Thirdly, Costa ignored the anti-Semitic manifestations of Italian society that surfaced
in the affair of the abducted Jewish child Edgardo Mortara, which occurred in 1858,
seven years after the publication of his book. See: David I Kertzer. The Kidnapping of
Edgardo Mortara. 1977.
A further important point should be considered. In group E Costa relates to the stories
of the people of Israel as a nation, whereas in group F he deals with the fate of individuals rather than with the destiny of entire Jewish communities. The individuals are generally famous Jewish figures such as Elijah Montalto and Jean Baptiste Silva, who do
not accurately represent the status of Jews within West European nations. Alphonse 264
Picard, who sacrificed himself in the 1830 revolution, did not represent the behavior of
the Jews of France in that revolution, since they did not participate in it. See: Zosa
Szajkowski. Jews and the French Revolutions of 1789, 1830 and 1848. 1970, p.1002.
Costa wished to instill in his pupils the idea that Jews could integrate in Italian society
and in other Western countries while preserving their Jewish identity. In other works,
Costa expressed his identification with the Italian nation, which was beginning to fight
for its independence and unification.
Costa relates a tale about a brave Jewish soldier in Napoleon's army and about Picard,
who died in the revolution of July 1830. He also brought stories from the ancient past
in which Jews are described as brave warriors (stories no. 12, 85 and 89). These stories
are intended to show that Jews were capable of fighting fearlessly and would be willing
to fight for Italy.
Carlotta Ferrara showed that the Jewish press in Italy during the second half of the
nineteenth century and at the turn of the twentieth century recalled the bravery of the
Maccabees and of contemporary Jews in order to show that Jews were willing and capable of fighting and dying for their fatherland, the ultimate test of patriotism. Ferrara:
2017, Ch. 5.
Costa also included stories which show that Jews were willing to die for Kiddush Hashem rather than contravening major mitzvot (stories no. 10, 17, 52, 53, 60, 85, 86, 87
and 99). Ferrara showed that similar stories appeared in Jewish discourse during the
nineteenth century. There is, however, an important difference between them and
Costa’s tales. Costa believed that Kiddush Hashem was a phenomenon of the past, since
Christians no longer sought to convert Jews, whereas the modern discourse as described
by Ferrara maintained that this phenomenon was still prevalent in the present. It was
now a symbol of patriotism: the willingness of Jews to die for the fatherland has a
connotation of dying for Kiddush Hashem:
"…the Jewish warriors of old had been located within the discursive and symbolic
sphere of nationalism and patriotism…These stories with a warlike setting went together with a rhetoric of sacrifice: alongside military courage were celebrated the valour
and moral integrity of the martyr." Ferrara: 2017, p. 179. 265
It appears that Costa’s optimistic conception regarding the status of Jews in Italy was
shared by many Jews in Italy. Historians who wrote before the rise of fascism in Italy
and before the horrors of the Holocaust likewise described in rosy colors the process of
emancipation of the Jews in Italy. It was only after the dark period in modern Jewish
history that historians began to reevaluate the process of emancipation and discovered
that it had not run all that smoothly and that there had been significant manifestations
of antisemitism, in which the Vatican and other groups in Italian society took part.
I am relying on Elizabeth Schachter's remarks: "Until recently, scholars of Italian history also subscribed to the view that Italy was an oasis of peaceful coexistence between
the Jews and the host society. In the two last decades, a reappraisal of the Racial Laws
of 1938 has led several historians to consider their implementation not as a rupture with
the past, but as a continuation of a tradition of clerical anti-Judaism arising from the
consequences of emancipation." Schachter 2011, p. 97.
Carlotta Ferrara made the same observation: "Scholars systematically deconstructed the
longstanding myth of an idyllic and unproblematic nineteenth-century integration of
the Jews into Italian society. This idea had its roots in the way Italian Jews had portrayed their belonging to the fatherland and their relationship with non-Jews." Carlotta
Ferrara: 2017, p. ix.
Both scholars rely on: Paolo Bernardini. "The Jews in nineteenth-century Italy: Towards a reappraisal.” Journal of Modern Italian Studies. 1, 2, 1996, pp. 292-310.
A reservation should be noted here: It could be argued that Costa was aware of the true
situation of the Jews in modern times, but preferred to present to his pupils an idyllic
picture, as he did in many stories in his anthology. I feel that he truly believed in these
ideas, as expressed in his poems and his views on the affair of Nissim Samama's will.
See Appendix II.
Source and Copy
Much of the interest that the anthology raises lies in Costa's tendency to rephrase his
sources and to modify and customize them to fit his didactic purposes. I wish firstly to
point out a recurring pattern of change that Costa introduced to his stories. He sought
to present to his pupils an idyllic reality, perhaps to spare them the harsh circumstances 266
that prevailed. Following are examples of significant changes he made in several stories
that stem from this motivation:
Story no. 57: every reader of the story of Rabbi Meir and the death of his children
according to the version of Yalkut Shim'oni cannot help but notice that the sage was
irked by his wife's manipulation and that he did not find complete solace in the parable
of the deposit. His silence in view of the situation is a thunderous silence that evokes
his dissatisfaction. Costa ignores this element and retells the story according to Midrash
Mishlei, according to which Rabbi Meir accepted the verdict with good grace, and took
no exception to the convoluted manner in which his wife chose to break the bad news
to him.
Story no. 58: in the Chazalic sources Yannai, who was called to serve as a witness in
the trial of his slave, refused to comply because he viewed it as an insult to his lofty
status as a king. Costa sugarcoated the story, in which Yannai agreed wholeheartedly
to serve as a witness, as he sought to instill in young readers the idea of equality before
law.
Story no. 89: nowadays, almost all references to Josephus Flavius raise the question of
whether he betrayed his people. Costa, however, presents him as a paragon of virtue,
as an ideal figure with whom his pupils can identify.
Story no. 41: according to Chazal, Abraham broke the statues and was consequently
thrown by Nimrod into a furnace. This raises an issue: if Abraham’s belief in monotheism was justified, how come he failed to convince the idolaters who threw him into the
fire? He surely did not deserve this fate, and Costa therefore sugarcoated the outcome:
Abraham convinced the idolaters that his faith was supreme and they bowed down and
declared: "The Lord is God.".
Story no. 23: this story, in which the archbishop increased his donation to the poor
woman when he realized that she was Jewish, was intended to convey the general message of group F. However, this differs from the interpretation of the Christian sources
that recalled the event. They sought to show the church’s generosity and tolerance toward the poor, with no distinction among nations, religions, or Christian divisions
(Catholics, Protestants, etc.) 267
The previous argument points to a connection between two editorial trends that Drori
(2018) has also identified: poetic license and the avoidance of moral dilemmas, and the
desire to convey clear-cut messages.
Costa’s stories invariably have a happy end; people who utter heresy keep silent after
hearing counter arguments. The central theme of all these stories is the idea of repentance: the sinner always repents and returns to the righteous path.
The happy end is typical of didactic literature. Great literature (including the Bible)
portrays evil characters who remain evil to the end of their lives. This point reinforces
the conclusion that the main purpose of the book is educational and that literary considerations were secondary.
The picture of the world that Costa paints for his young readers is an idyllic one. The
stories of group F should be seen in this perspective. In the modern era, gentiles did not
welcome assimilation or conversion of the Jews and praised Jews who observed the
Jewish religion and maintained their Jewish identity and culture.
Costa uses poetic license to further his didactic ends. Yet we should remember that he
achieves this goal primarily by deciding in the first place which stories to include in his
anthology and which to leave out. For example, he did not choose stories that showed
that hatred of the Jews had not ceased in modern times.
Costa furthermore found it important to emphasize in various stories that Jews were
lauded by major gentile figures. The underlying message in these stories is that Jews
can integrate into Italian society while maintaining their Jewish identity and they will
be welcomed into it.
Costa was eager to show that Jews could undertake extraordinary deeds (involving
bravery or exemplary brotherhood, for example). To this end he even took gentiles and
"converted" them to Judaism. The most conspicuous example of this is the story about
the brave acrobat that Costa turned into an Israelita (story no. 30).
Did Costa convert the acrobat because he was from Troyes, the city of Rashi, or was he
seeking to fire the imagination of his pupils to show them that a Jew could be an acrobat
or an exemplary figure? 268
The acrobat displayed human and civic courage, but in another story the hero displayed
bravery on the battlefield and readiness to die for the fatherland. I am referring to Picard, who was killed in the 1830 revolution in Paris (story no. 76). It is possible that
Picard was not a Jew and that Costa "converted" him. This tale belongs to a group of
stories in which Costa sought to convey the message that the Jews of Italy wished to
take part in the Risorgimento and were capable of doing so. The stories in that group
are: 35, 76, 77 and 83.
Worthy of note here is the story about Dama ben Netina (story no. 62), who honored
his father in an exemplary way. The reader gains the impression that this hero is a Jew,
while in fact he was a gentile jeweler from Ashkelon.
An further example is the famous legend of the two brothers and the location of the
Temple – story no. 59. Costa knew that the source of the story was Arabic. It is almost
an identical translation of the legend that Alphonse de Lamartine, a French poet and
statesman, heard from an Arab during his visit to Jerusalem in 1832, on a voyage to the
Levant. (Alphonse de Lamartine. Voyage en Orient. Paris: Librairie de Charles
Gosselin,1843 (1835). pp. 435-436.
De Lamartine's Visit to the Holy Land or Recollections of the East. Vol. I. London:
George Virtue. 1845. pp. 333-334.
Costa "converted" the story by employing biblical allusions and referring in the opening
sentence to "the place in which our holy and glorious house was built." The reader is
thus led to believe that the two generous brothers are Jews, whereas in the original
source their nationality is not stated.
On this legend, which was extensively studied, see: Appendix B: "The Legend of the
Brothers and the Temple Location." (in Hebrew).
Some of the biographies that Costa brought to his readers are folk legends, which are
not based on facts. For example, he said of Rashi (story 94) that he was knowledgeable
in philosophy and commanded many languages, including Greek. He sought to present
Rashi as an ideal figure: a man who masters the main texts of the Jewish religion but is
also knowledgeable in general fields of study. 269
He likewise included a folk legend pertaining to the childhood of Maimonides: Maimonides the child was a very slow learner and his father threw him out. He studied the
Torah for years with various rabbis and only then, as a learned person, did he return to
meet his father. The message to the slow learning pupil is thus: do not lose hope, perhaps you will be revealed as a genius if you persist in your studies. (There are similar
stories about Albert Einstein's childhood).
Costa employed the technique of conflating two different stories from unrelated sources
in two of his stories. The first is story no. 41 about Abraham and the idolaters. Abraham
was not thrown into the fire because of his alleged heresy, as in the original source, and
in Costa's version the idolaters bowed and confessed: " The Lord, He is God," just like
the people of Israel after the confrontation of Elijah with the prophets of Ba'al on
Mount Carmel (I Kings 18: 39).
The second story, no. 98, is about the Nazirite from the South. Here Costa uses a Chazalic source as well as the story about Narcissus from Greek mythology.
The Human Axis
The stories of the anthology revolve around a Jewish axis and a human axis. This section deals with the human axis.
Costa wanted his anthology to be relevant to his young readers. First, a quarter of the
stories deal with children. Second, more than a fifth of the stories – 23 – are set in the
family and six at school. Third, 40 percent of the issues dealt with in the anthology
relate to the family and education. This finding is consistent with the fact that the world
of children revolves around the family and the school. Fourth, one fifth of the stories
commend learning and education.
One may assume that Costa’s young readers were aware of the social class of their
parents, since it impacted their diet, their clothes, their social standing among their
peers, and the attitude of their teachers toward them. Therefore, it is not surprising that
a third of the stories deal with poor and/or rich people. 270
A fifth of the stories belong to group C: the inculcation of the virtues: loyalty and solidarity within the family, learning and acquisition of knowledge, charity and philanthropy, diligence at school or at work, adhering to the truth and steering clear of theft
and fraud, and the protagonist’s remorse for his misconduct.
Costa generally encourages conformity and mediocrity among his pupils. My conclusion is based on the fact that in all the stories those who digressed or questioned the
tenets of the Jewish faith ultimately express regret for their actions and beliefs, repent,
and realign themselves with the conventions.
Although I distinguish between the human axis and the Jewish axis, for Costa they are
intertwined and he tends to validate the human axis by linking it to the Jewish faith, as
in the ten commandments.
The Language of the Stories
Costa employs biblical Hebrew, in accordance with the convention in nineteenth-century Jewish enlightenment literature. (See Benjamin Hershav: 2008 (in Hebrew)).
Costa’s numerous biblical allusions in the anthology constitute an essential linguistic
and literary technique on his part.
The Addressee
I deal here with the messages that Costa sought to convey to his young readers. Yet in
every act of communication the addressee can completely ignore the messages, willingly accept them, or rebel against them, and he might also interpret them in a different
way to that conceived by the addresser. (On Roman Jakobson's model of communication, see his essay: "Closing Statement: Linguistics and Poetics." In Thomas A. Sebeok
(ed.). Style in Language. 1960, pp. 350-377).
Since we have no information about Costa’s addressees, our research must remain incomplete. An anecdote will clarify this: My five year-old daughter came to us – her
parents – a few days before Passover Seder (in Tel Aviv, 1980) and asked: "Who are
those Jews that the kindergarten teacher tells us so much about?" We were surprised
(and frankly also amused) by the question, because both the kindergarten teacher and
we assumed that children of her age should know who the Jews in the Passover myths 271
are. The lesson is clear: there are two sides to every communication and I have focused
only on one side.
In conclusion: I hope I have succeeded in demonstrating the messages that Costa
sought to deliver to his pupils through his anthology. Those messages were in line with
